Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in a subset of liver cancers, the simultaneous overexpression of SF3B2 and dysregulation of its co-factors SF3B1 and SF3B4 not only results in the aberrant splicing of DNA repair genes such as TP53 and RAD51, but also triggers a reprogramming of the chromatin landscape—possibly via dysregulated expression of chromatin modifiers. This chromatin remodeling creates an open, permissive environment that facilitates the integration of hepatotropic viral genomes (e.g., HBV and HCV). Such integration events exacerbate genomic instability, thereby activating oncogenic signaling cascades including those promoting metastasis and angiogenesis, ultimately resulting in poor clinical outcomes in liver neoplasms. We will address this hypothesis by using CRISPR interference to modulate the expression levels of SF3B2, SF3B1, and SF3B4, complemented by single-cell RNA sequencing and long-read sequencing to delineate the splicing variants and viral integration patterns, as well as chromatin immunoprecipitation and functional assays to assess DNA repair capacity and chromatin accessibility.
Abstract: Liver cancer remains a leading cause of cancer‐related mortality, and splicing dysregulation has emerged as a critical contributor to its pathogenesis. We propose that in a distinct subset of liver neoplasms, the overexpression of SF3B2 together with co-dysregulation of SF3B1 and SF3B4 drives not only the generation of aberrant splice variants of key DNA repair regulators such as TP53 and RAD51, but also induces alterations in the chromatin landscape that enhance the accessibility of hepatotropic viral DNA (e.g., HBV/HCV) to the host genome. This cascade of events—beginning with misregulated splicing factor expression, progressing to defective DNA repair and chromatin remodeling, and culminating in increased viral integration—underpins a novel mechanism linking splicing abnormalities to genomic instability and oncogenic signaling (including metastasis and angiogenesis). Our experimental framework leverages contemporary technologies such as high-throughput and single-cell RNA sequencing to capture splicing heterogeneity, CRISPR interference tools for precise modulation of splicing factor expression, long-read sequencing for the accurate mapping of viral integration sites, and advanced chromatin immunoprecipitation assays to monitor histone modification patterns. This integrative approach will clarify the causal impact of splicing defects on chromatin state changes and viral integration in liver neoplasms.
CausalChain: SF3B2 upregulation + SF3B1/SF3B4 dysregulation -> Aberrant splicing of TP53 and RAD51 (and other regulatory genes) -> Impaired DNA repair and altered expression of chromatin remodelers -> Modified chromatin landscape (increased accessibility) -> Enhanced susceptibility to viral DNA integration -> Genomic instability -> Activation of metastasis and angiogenesis -> Poor liver neoplasm prognosis
